summary: An April 1st joke RFC specifying how to send IPv4 and IPv6 packets using the Semaphore Flag Signaling System, with people waving flags. It is humorous and not meant for real deployment.

eli5.summary: This is a joke: send internet messages by having people wave flags, like sailors. It is slow and silly, and published for April Fools' Day.

subtitle: Joke protocol for transmitting IP packets using semaphore flags

tldr.problem: This is an April Fools' joke proposing that IPv4 and IPv6 packets can be transmitted using the Semaphore Flag Signaling System, where people wave hand-held flags to represent data.
tldr.mechanism: IP-SFS encodes IP datagrams as 4-bit nibbles, each represented by a specific semaphore flag pattern. Data signals (A-P) represent nibbles 0-15, while control signals (Q-X) handle framing and flow control. A human operator waves the appropriate flags in sequence to transmit the packet.
tldr.outcome: This is a humorous RFC. No actual IP over semaphore flag systems were deployed. The joke highlights that the Internet Protocol can theoretically work over any transport medium, even an absurdly impractical one.

today: This is an April Fools' joke from 2007. IP over semaphore flags has never been deployed in any Internet infrastructure. The RFC remains on record as an Informational document.

sections.title: IP over Flags
sections.content:
RFC 4824 presents itself as a serious technical specification, claiming that IPv4 and IPv6 packets can be transmitted over SFSS (Semaphore Flag Signaling System)—a communication method based on waving pairs of hand-held flags. The physical layer uses 'optical transmission, normally through the atmosphere using solar illumination and line-of-sight photonics', in other words, the human eye.

The humor lies in treating this absurdly impractical system as if it were a legitimate Internet transport layer, complete with detailed framing specifications, checksums, and flow control algorithms.
sections.eli5: Imagine sending emails by having someone stand on a hill waving flags. That is what this joke document describes, with all the serious technical details you would normally see for real internet protocols.

sections.title: Encoding and Signals
sections.content:
IP-SFS encodes data in 4-bit nibbles, two per octet. The 16 data signals correspond to semaphore flag patterns for letters A through P, representing hex values 0x00 through 0x0F. Each flag pattern shows a stick figure with two flags in a specific position to represent a nibble.

The protocol includes nine control signals (Q through X) for frame delimitation and flow control, with names like FST (Frame Start), FEN (Frame End), ACK, NAK, and humorously, SUN (Signal UNdo) and FUN (Frame UNdo). The RFC specifies that bit error rates depend on the operator's skill level, ranging from 1e-3 for a 'boy scout' to 1e-4 for a 'professional sailor'.
sections.eli5: Each flag movement represents a number (0-15). Different movements mean 'start frame', 'end frame', or 'okay I got it'. The joke includes silly details like how boy scouts are worse at this than professional sailors.

sections.title: Implementation and Physical Constraints
sections.content:
The RFC specifies that 'an interface is constructed through the participation of one or more humans' and notes that 'knowledge of the SFSS is recommended, but its absence can be compensated by a well-designed GUI'—the idea being that a computer could tell a human what flags to wave.

The protocol has severe limitations: frames are limited to 255 octets of payload per frame (510 nibbles), datagrams can be fragmented across at most 255 frames, and the entire system is unusable in poor visibility or at night. The RFC deadpan notes that the protocol is 'not suitable in environments where interfaces are moving fast and/or when the path of light is long'.
sections.eli5: A human needs to do the waving, but a computer could tell them which flags to wave. You cannot do this at night, in fog, or when people are moving around. The whole thing is impractical and that is the joke.

references.text: Bradner, S., "Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels", BCP 14, RFC 2119, March 1997.
